title: Nobody read our weekly product doc, so our CTO made a 4-minute video
summary: Our CTO's weekly product doc went mostly unread. A 4-minute video got 17 hearts and a real thread from sales and CS. What changed, and how to try it.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- Our product team ships fast, and sales, CS, and marketing need to know what's coming before it lands. That's product enablement, and at Clueso it was running on a weekly Notion doc.
- The doc was thorough but mostly unread.
- PJ posted a 4-minute video next to it, with customer-facing changes first and the under-the-hood stuff last. People watched it, and sales and CS started asking real questions about support and pricing in the thread.
- The video didn't replace the doc. It got people to actually use it.
- You can try this with the doc you already write. Keep it under five minutes and put what customers will notice first.


Most Mondays the past few months, our CTO, Prajwal, would send the same Slack message on our general channel: "@here Please go through this document!"


Under it was a link to a Notion page with a name like "Product Summary — 2 Nov".


I'll be honest, I didn't always go through the document. (Sorry, PJ!). And it seemed like I had company. His message usually got one or two reactions before people scrolled past it.


Last week PJ tried something different. Next to the doc, he posted a 4-minute video walking through what the product team was building.


This is the kind of response his video received:


Naturally, PJ was really pleased with the responses:


## Shipping fast makes product enablement harder, not easier


Our product team has gotten really good at shipping quickly. Over the same stretch, marketing, sales, and CS have all grown a lot. That's a good problem to have, but it's still a problem: more people need to know what's changing, especially when things are changing faster.


Product enablement is the work of making sure the people who sell, support, and market a product understand what's changing in it, why it's changing, and what to tell customers. Ideally they learn it before a customer asks them.


At our size (we're 41 people), nobody owns that job full time. So it landed on PJ. In his words, "keeping everyone in sync has become an important part of my job."


- Sales wants to know what to say to a prospect about next month.
- CS wants to warn customers before a screen they use every day moves.
- Marketing needs enough notice to plan a launch.


## Weekly product docs can be thorough, but not everyone may read it


We make most of our product decisions at the start of the week. So every Monday, after a pile of pod meetings, PJ usually writes everything up in Notion: what we're building, why, what to expect, and who to talk to for more detail.


It's a good doc. It's organized and complete, and it has a "Starting this week" section and a "Deployments" section so you could find your way around.


But given how fast things move, not everyone has time to navigate a doc and find parts that matter to them the most.


And to be honest, there's no one to blame for this. We don't think the doc was the problem either. According to PJ: "A long, slightly technical document isn't something you look forward to on a Monday."


If you're in sales, you open it, see a wall of bullets about deployments, and decide you'll read it later. That later never comes, and soon enough there's a new doc next Monday.


## Why the video worked when the doc didn't (my best guesses)


I've thought about this a fair bit, mostly because I write content for a living and I'd like to know when nobody's reading it. These are my guesses, not research.


- People need something more engaging than a doc, especially when it's about a product.
- Most people in our company (and the B2B world at large, I believe) are using their agents to retrieve and synthesize information. For that, documents work far better since they're easy to retrieve by agents.


But when it comes to understanding how a feature is being built or how it works in a product, it's better to show it than just write about it and expect people to read.


You can see the product in action and it's especially helpful if you're in Sales or CS and you havAtte to navigate the product or a new feature yourself during calls.


Videos are also more engaging because it feels like someone talking to you, and people respond to it better.


## How can you make a weekly product update video for your own team


If you already write a weekly update, you've done the hard part. The video is a different way of delivering something you already have.


1. **Keep writing the doc.** The video goes next to it, not instead of it. More on that below.
2. **Reorder for the people watching.** Lead with what customers will see or ask about. Infrastructure, refactors, and internal tooling go last.
3. **Keep it under five minutes.** PJ's ran four. If it's running long, there's probably a change that only one team cares about, and that one can stay in the doc.
4. **Say who to ask.** The doc's "who to talk to" section is the most useful part for sales and CS, so keep it in the video.
5. **Post it where the conversation already happens.** Put it in the same thread as the doc, in the channel your sales and CS teams already read.


The part that usually stops people is making the video. Most PMs and engineering leads don't edit video, and a weekly update can't wait for a creative team. You don't need either. If you connect the[Clueso MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or Cursor, you can give your agent the doc you already wrote (a PDF, a DOCX, or a URL) and ask it for a short update video. It builds the video in your Clueso workspace, and it stays fully editable, by hand or by chat. To change one thing, like zooming in on a new setting or cutting a section, tell[Clueso's editing agent](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) and it makes that one edit without touching the rest.


> **Try it:** connect the[Clueso MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) to the AI assistant you already use, and turn this week's product doc into a 4-minute update.


## Should you replace your docs with videos? (No)


PJ didn't. He posted the video *next to* the doc, and I think that's the right call.


The doc is still the thing you search when a customer asks about a change three weeks later. It's where the links, the ticket numbers, and the detail the engineers care about live. The video's job is different: it gets people to understand updates quickly and tells them which parts of the doc they need to open.


PJ ended his post with this, and I agree with him: "Sometimes another Notion doc, another meeting, or enforcing SOPs, isn't the answer." Sometimes the doc is fine, and it needs a short video in front of it.


If you're doing this for the whole company rather than for GTM teams, our guide to[internal communications videos employees will actually watch](https://www.clueso.io/blog/internal-communications-videos) covers CEO updates and org changes. For updates going out to customers, see[release-note videos vs. written changelogs](https://www.clueso.io/blog/release-note-videos-vs-changelogs) .


## Frequently asked questions


### What is product enablement?


Product enablement is making sure the people who sell, support, and market a product understand what's changing in it, why, and what to tell customers. In a small company it usually falls to a product lead or a PMM, through weekly updates, launch briefs, and demos. Clueso helps by turning those updates into short videos: with the[Clueso MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) , your AI assistant can build one from the doc you already wrote.


### How long should an internal product update video be?


Under five minutes is a good target. PJ's ran four and covered a full week of product decisions. Put the customer-facing changes first so people who stop early still get what they need.


### Should a product update video replace internal release notes?


No. Keep the written notes for search, links, and detail, and post the video alongside them. In our case the video is what got people engaging with the update at all, and the doc stayed the reference.


### How do you make a product update video without editing skills?


Start from the written update. With the[Clueso MCP](https://www.clueso.io/mcp) connected to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or Cursor, you can give the agent your doc and ask for a short video. It builds it in your Clueso workspace, where you or the agent can edit it. For smaller changes,[Clueso's editing agent](https://www.clueso.io/features/clueso-agents) makes one edit at a time and leaves the rest of the video as it was.


If you already post a weekly product doc, try this next Monday: record four minutes on the changes customers will notice first, post it under the doc, and see what the thread looks like. Ours went from one or two emoji to sales and CS asking how we'd support and price a feature.
